name: BFS tree by agents

origin.note: BFS without root knowledge in the agent-based model (SSS 2025).

summary: $n$ agents in an anonymous graph must build a breadth-first spanning tree, without being told the root.
statement: $n$ agents with distinct identifiers (IDs) are placed on the nodes of an anonymous port-labelled graph with $n$ nodes, $m$ edges and maximum degree $\Delta$. The start is rooted (all agents on one node), dispersed (one agent on each node) or arbitrary. Agents compute only by moving and by talking with agents on the same node. The agents must build a BFS tree from a root they choose, each agent knowing its parent and children: every agent (or node) learns its part of the output. **Time** is in synchronous rounds; **memory** in bits per agent.

primer.intro: Imagine $n$ **agents** (small mobile computers), one in each room of a building, who want a plan for emergencies: one room is the exit, and every other agent should know which room next to its own is one step closer to the exit along a shortest route. The building is a **graph**: rooms are its **nodes** and corridors are its **edges**; there are $n$ nodes and $m$ edges, and from here on we say only node and edge. Two nodes joined by an edge are *neighbours*. The **degree** of a node is the number of edges at it, $\Delta$ is the maximum degree, and the *diameter* $D$ is the largest distance between two nodes. Nodes have no names, but the edges at a node are numbered $1, 2, \dots$; these numbers are **ports**. A **BFS tree** (breadth-first search tree) with **root** $s$ (the exit of the picture) gives every other node $v$ a **parent**: a neighbour of $v$ that is one step closer to $s$, so following parents gives a shortest path to $s$. In the basic version the agents start one per node (a **dispersed** start; an agent's starting node is its **home**), have distinct **identifiers** (IDs), know nothing about the graph, and must choose the root themselves; they move in synchronous **rounds** (talk to the agents on the same node, then move along at most one edge), and at the end every agent knows its parent and its children. We count rounds and bits of memory per agent. As for all problems in this family, agents can imitate message-passing algorithms by visiting neighbours, the method explained under leader election by agents.

ideas.title: Grow the tree layer by layer from a known root
ideas.idea:
Suppose the agent on the root $s$ is already known and the agents know $\Delta$. Time is cut into phases of $2\Delta$ rounds. Each agent will record a **depth**, a number that is unknown at the start.

1. In phase 0 the root agent takes depth 0.
2. In phase $d$, every agent of depth $d$ visits its neighbours one by one (out along one edge, back along it); all other agents stay at home.
3. An agent that has no depth yet and receives such a visit takes depth $d+1$ and records the visitor's home as its parent (if several visitors arrive, it picks the smallest ID). The visitor records its new child.
4. Repeat with phase $d+1$ until no agent gets a new depth.
ideas.analysis: An agent gets depth $d$ exactly when its distance to $s$ is $d$, so the parents form a BFS tree. During phase $d$ only depth-$d$ agents move, so the agents they visit are at home. Each phase lasts $2\Delta$ rounds and there are at most $D$ phases with new nodes, so the tree is built in $O(D\Delta)$ rounds; [Chand2025Trees] cite this bound for a known root. Without a known root they first build an MST to get a root and the values $m$ and $\Delta$, which gives $O(\min(D\Delta, m\log n) + n\log n + \Delta\log^2 n)$ rounds with $O(\log n)$ bits.
ideas.why_it_matters: It is the agent version of the textbook BFS, and it shows why knowing $\Delta$ matters: it fixes how long a phase must last.

ideas.title: A BFS tree contains an elected leader
ideas.idea: When a BFS tree has been built, the agent on the root knows it has no parent, and every other agent knows it has one. So "I am the root" is exactly a leader election: one agent knows it is the leader and all others know they are not.
ideas.analysis: Hence building a BFS tree without a known root is at least as hard as leader election, and any lower bound for leader election also holds for BFS. This is why the best known algorithm spends $O(n\log n + \Delta\log^2 n)$ rounds electing a leader (via an MST) before the BFS itself [Chand2025Trees]. The catalogue records no lower bound for either problem, so the time this preliminary step really needs is open.
ideas.why_it_matters: It explains why leader election is the first building block in this family: trees, MIS and counting all need an agent that starts things off.

glossary.definition: the connected, undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ on which the agents move, with $n$ nodes and $m$ edges; it is anonymous: its nodes carry no names that an agent can read
an element of $V$; nodes are anonymous
an element of $E$, joining two nodes (which are then neighbours); an agent crosses one edge in one round
the local number $1, \dots, \deg(v)$ that a node $v$ gives to each edge incident to it; the two ends of an edge may carry different numbers
$\deg(v)$, the number of edges at node $v$; $\Delta$ is the maximum degree
a mobile computing entity that moves along edges, talks only with the agents on its own node, and keeps its memory between rounds
the distinct positive integer, at most $L$, that each agent carries; written ID
a synchronous step in which every agent first talks with the agents on its node and then moves along at most one edge
with exactly one agent on every node; a dispersed start begins so, and to disperse is to reach this configuration
the node on which an agent of a dispersed configuration stays, and to which it returns after each visit to a neighbour
a breadth-first search tree of $G$ with root $s$: a spanning tree in which the path from every node to $s$ is a shortest path of $G$
the node $s$ of the BFS tree that has no parent; here it is not given and the agents choose it
for a node $v \neq s$, the neighbour of $v$ that is one step closer to the root $s$ in the BFS tree; the nodes whose parent is $v$ are its children
the number an agent records in the layer-by-layer algorithm: $0$ at the root and $d+1$ for an agent first visited in phase $d$; it equals the distance from its home to the root

history: BFS trees are the next building block after leader election; the question is **rounds then memory** without knowledge of the root or of graph parameters [Chand2025Trees].

axes.name: Knowledge

values.label: $n$ and $\Delta$ are known
values.definition: Every agent knows $n$ and $\Delta$ (upper bounds suffice where stated).

axes.origin: Whether agents know global parameters is inherited from message passing, where nodes typically know $n$ or an upper bound on it, and possibly $\Delta$ and $D$; Kshemkalyani, Kumar, Molla and Sharma set the agent-based model against this and asked for algorithms that rely on no such knowledge, "neither exact nor an upper bound" [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE]. Knowing $n$ and $\Delta$ tells an agent how long to wait: in the arbitrary-start minimal dominating set algorithm of Chand, Molla and Sivasubramaniam every robot waits $\kappa n\Delta$ rounds before leader election begins [Chand2023Cover], and the introductory maximal independent set algorithm assumes both $n$ and $\Delta$ [Pattanayak2024MIS] (as reported by [Kaur2026MIS] and [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE]). Kshemkalyani et al. state the trade-off: solutions without knowledge "are more resilient to network changes and device faults", but "algorithm design becomes challenging since devices may not know how long to run a procedure to guarantee a solution" [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE]. Later papers remove the assumption by first dispersing with termination detection and electing a leader, after which a spanning tree lets the agents compute $\Delta$ and the largest identifier themselves [Chand2026Triangle]; knowing only that largest identifier $L$ is a weaker assumption, recorded on results rather than as a level of this axis [Chand2025Trees]. For BFS trees the catalogued algorithm uses no graph parameter, only $L$ [Chand2025Trees].

variants.title: Dispersed start, root unknown
variants.summary: A BFS tree in $O(\min(D\Delta, m\log n)+n\log n+\Delta\log^2 n)$ rounds with $O(\log n)$ bits.

results.note: Introductory and current best without knowledge of the root; $O(D\Delta)$ was known with a known root.

figure.caption: BFS tree, grown layer by layer [Chand2025Trees]: the agents are dispersed and the root (agent 1, chosen by leader election, not shown) has depth 0. In phase $d$ (of $2\Delta = 6$ rounds) every agent of depth $d$ visits each neighbour and comes back, one edge per round, while all others wait at home; a waiting agent without a depth that is visited takes depth $d+1$ and the visitor's home as its parent (thick edges). The tree is complete when a phase gives no new depth.
